sections.h2: What makes selling a house in Nashville different from other Tennessee cities?
sections.html:
Nashville and Davidson County share one government, so a house sale touches a single set of offices: the Assessor of Property, the Metropolitan Trustee and the Register of Deeds. Three small cities, Belle Meade, Ridgetop and Goodlettsville, bill their own city tax, and everything else in the county is billed by the Trustee. The county seat sits on the Cumberland River in the Nashville Basin, and the ground rises into the Highland Rim on the west side of town. The city is very hilly, so expect sloped lots.

The Census Bureau counts 721,074 people in the Nashville-Davidson balance as of July 1, 2025, up 4.6% from the April 2020 base. Only 52.4% of housing units are owner-occupied, so a large share of sellers here are investors, landlords and heirs rather than long-term residents. Use the table below to see which office handles which part of a sale.

OfficeWhat a seller needs from itWhere and when
Register of DeedsRecords the deed and collects the state recording tax300 Deaderick St, Monday to Friday, 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.
Metropolitan TrusteeBills and collects property tax700 President Ronald Reagan Way, Suite 220, 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.
Assessor of PropertySets the appraised value and hears informal reviews615-862-6080 for assessment questions
Codes AdministrationIssues short term rental permitsApplications run through the Metro Codes site

Sources for the table: the Register of Deeds and the Trustee's property tax FAQ.

sections.h2: What do Census figures say about Nashville homeowners?
sections.html:
The median value of an owner-occupied home in the Nashville-Davidson balance is $413,600 for 2020 to 2024, and median gross rent is $1,586. The city holds 313,513 households with an average of 2.13 people each, which points to many one and two person homes. About 80.7% of residents lived in the same house a year earlier, so churn is lower than the headline growth suggests.

  • Bachelor's degree or higher: 48.0% of adults age 25 and over
  • Mean travel time to work: 24.7 minutes
  • Median household income: $77,371 in 2024 dollars
  • Persons in poverty: 14.1%

These numbers come from Census QuickFacts. They describe the city as a whole, so a single street or condo building can look very different.

sections.h2: How did the 2025 reappraisal change Nashville tax bills?
sections.html:
The Assessor mailed new values on April 18, 2025, and the countywide median increase was 45%. Council district medians ranged from 38% to 54%. The Assessor says the reappraisal was revenue neutral by law, but Metro then raised the rate to $2.814 per $100 of assessed value in the Urban Services District and $2.782 in the General Services District, increases of 26% and 39% over the certified rates. Owners can appeal a value, but they cannot appeal the rate.

A house appraised at $100,000 is assessed at 25%, or $25,000, so the Trustee's own example works out to $703.50 in the Urban Services District and $695.50 in the General Services District. Scale that to a Nashville house at the Census median value of $413,600 and the same arithmetic gives roughly $2,909 and $2,876 a year. The informal review deadline for 2025 was May 9 and the formal appeal deadline was June 27, so both have passed. Ask the Assessor at 615-862-6059 how to challenge a value in a later year.

sections.h2: When are Nashville property taxes due, and who pays at closing?
sections.html:
Metro tax statements go out the first week of October. Taxes are due on the first Monday of October and can be paid without interest through the last day of February. From March 1, interest of 1.5% a month is added to the base tax. Partial payments are accepted, and a card payment carries a 2.55% fee with a $2.00 minimum.

The Trustee notes that the October bill covers the current calendar year and goes to the owner of record. New owners should check the closing statement to see who covers which months, because unpaid tax stays attached to the property. If you sell in the fall, ask the title company to confirm whether the current year's bill has been paid or prorated.

  • Tax bills are not required to be mailed, so a missed bill does not excuse interest.
  • Mail payments are dated by postmark, and office meter dates do not count.
  • Delinquent parcels can end up in a tax sale, with a one year right to redeem.

sections.h2: Is there property tax relief for an older or disabled Nashville owner?
sections.html:
Davidson County runs both tax relief and a tax freeze. For tax year 2026 the Comptroller lists the freeze income limit for Davidson County at $54,900, and the Trustee says an applicant must turn 65 by December 31 of the tax year. Disabled veterans with a 100% rating have no income limit, and relief applies to the first $175,000 of market value.

If you are selling a home that carries one of these programs, tell your buyer or title company early. Both programs turn on the owner's age, residence and income. Ask the Trustee at 615-862-6330 which paperwork to bring.

sections.h2: What happens at the Davidson County Register of Deeds when a house sells?
sections.html:
The deed is recorded at 300 Deaderick Street, and the office also offers remote filing and a fee calculator. State law puts a recording tax of $0.37 per $100 of price on the transfer. The office needs original, signed and notarized documents, and it cannot draft a deed for you or run a lien search, so those jobs go to an attorney or title company.

Ownership records here are searchable online by subscription, and the Register can tell you when a document was recorded and its reference number. You can get a copy of your own deed from the office at any time. For a quick sale, ask your buyer's title company to schedule recording the same day as closing so the new deed is indexed right away.

sections.h2: How do short term rental permits affect a Nashville sale?
sections.html:
A permit for a short term rental belongs to one owner and one address. Metro Codes says it cannot be transferred, and any change in ownership cancels it, including a move from a person to a trust or an LLC. So a buyer who wants to keep renting by the night must apply fresh instead of inheriting yours.

  • Permits expire 365 days after issue unless renewed.
  • Occupancy is capped at twice the number of sleeping rooms plus four, with a maximum of 12.
  • The principal renter must be at least 21.
  • The permit holder collects and remits room, occupancy and sales taxes.

If your house has an active permit, mention it in the listing or offer so the buyer knows it ends at closing. See the Metro Codes operating rules.

sections.h2: How old is Nashville, and does it matter to a seller?
sections.html:
Nashville grew from Fort Nashborough, built in 1779 on the Cumberland River. It was incorporated as a city in 1806, became the permanent state capital in 1843, and merged with Davidson County in 1963. Metro Nashville Public Schools lists 160 schools, and its history page notes that the first unified school board met on July 1, 1964.

That mix of old and new neighborhoods means houses range widely in age. Older homes often need a pre-sale look at roofs, foundations and wiring, and the Assessor's records can show you the year built and the square footage on file. Compare those details with what you know before you accept any price.

sections.h2: What are the ways to sell a house quickly in Nashville?
sections.html:
You can list with an agent, sell it yourself, or take a cash offer from a buyer who purchases as-is. Listing usually brings the widest pool of buyers but adds showings and repair requests. A cash buyer removes most of that, and closing can follow the title work rather than a lender's schedule.

Whichever route you choose, ask for the offer in writing, confirm who pays the recording tax and any back taxes, and have a title company handle the deed. If the house has liens, a tax bill in arrears or an expired short term rental permit, resolve those at closing so they do not follow you.

faqs.q: Do I owe a Nashville tax bill if I sell in the fall?
faqs.a: Usually yes for the part of the year you owned the house. The October bill covers the full calendar year and goes to the owner of record, so the closing statement should prorate it between you and the buyer.

faqs.q: Can I appeal the Nashville tax rate?
faqs.a: No. The Assessor says an owner can appeal a property value, but the rate is set by the Mayor and Metro Council. For 2025 those rates were $2.814 in the Urban Services District and $2.782 in the General Services District per $100 of assessed value.

faqs.q: What does the Register of Deeds charge to record a Nashville deed?
faqs.a: The state recording tax is $0.37 per $100 of price, plus a recording fee with a $10 minimum. Use the office's online fee calculator for a specific deed, since the total depends on page count and price.

faqs.q: Does my short term rental permit transfer to a buyer?
faqs.a: No. Metro Codes states a permit cannot be assigned to another person, entity or address, and a change of ownership cancels it. The buyer has to apply on their own.

faqs.q: Where do I pay Davidson County property tax in person?
faqs.a: The Trustee's office is in the Howard Office Building at 700 President Ronald Reagan Way, Suite 220, open Monday through Friday from 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. You can also pay online or by mail to PO Box 196358, Nashville, TN 37219-6358.
